title: The Supply Side of Social Media
abstract: We study social media’s distinctive model of content production. Unlike legacy media outlets, social media platforms do not professionally produce content optimized to appeal to viewers. Instead, they harvest the output of large numbers of amateur users creating content in pursuit of nonpecuniary rewards. The resulting scale and diversity of platforms’ content libraries, combined with their ability to experimentally test new content on subsets of viewers, allows them to ex-post discover the content most appealing to each viewer. We develop a model of this process and show that it leads the content consumed in equilibrium to depend on viewer preferences (demand) but also on creator preferences (supply), because the scale powering platforms’ discovery concentrates where creators are eager to produce. Collecting new data on Instagram, TikTok, and X/Twitter, we show that viewers’ feeds are dominated by unpaid amateurs who produce envy-provoking “lifestyle” and partisan political content in pursuit of social status and expressive satisfaction. We experimentally generate supply- and demand-side shifters by manipulating viewers’ feeds and eliciting creators’ incentivized preferences while paying them to produce content. On the demand side, pieces of lifestyle and partisan content are less likely to highly engage viewers than more benign entertainment. But these content types enjoy enormous supply-driven production scale. This enables platforms to cherry-pick the minority of such pieces viewers find more engaging than the marginal piece of entertainment. Estimating our model using the experimental variation, we calculate that supply-side preferences account for one- to two-thirds of the prevalence of lifestyle and partisan content in viewers’ feeds.
